title: Accessibility on a marketing site
excerpt: Contrast, keyboard focus, names on controls, and a way to stop motion are part of shipping. A marketing site that fails them is unfinished.
alt: A hand holding a stylus over a tablet covered in wireframe sketches, with a keyboard and mouse beside it. The keyboard in the frame fits a piece about a site that has to work without a pointer.
caption: A page you can only use with a mouse is not finished. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What does accessible mean on a marketing site?
faqs.answer: It means a stranger can perceive the offer, operate the page, and understand what will happen when they act. The W3C's WCAG 2 overview groups the standard under four principles: perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. On a company site that shows up as contrast, a visible focus, names on controls and images, and a way to stop motion.

faqs.question: Is accessibility a separate phase after launch?
faqs.answer: No. Retrofitting contrast, focus, and names after the visual design is locked costs more and usually leaves gaps. Put the checks in the same review as the copy and the mobile layout. A beautiful homepage that cannot be used from a keyboard is unfinished, even if the launch date has arrived.

faqs.question: Which level should a small team aim for?
faqs.answer: WCAG 2.2 is the version W3C encourages, and most teams treat AA success criteria as the working bar. The overview is the map, not a substitute for the criteria themselves. You do not need a lab to start. You need someone to tab through the page, read the headline at arm's length, and turn on reduced motion.

markdown:
An accessible marketing website is a finished website. Contrast, a visible focus, names on controls and images, and a way to stop motion are part of shipping. A page that only works for a person with a mouse, a quiet room, and perfect vision is a draft.

The W3C describes WCAG 2 as a shared standard for web content, organized under four principles: perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. WCAG 2.2 is the version W3C encourages. Conformance is a set of testable success criteria at levels A, AA, and AAA. You can hold a marketing site to that standard without turning the project into a research program. The four checks below are where founders actually feel the gap.

## Contrast and type you can read

Perceivable starts with the sentence. If the headline is pale gray on a photograph, some of your buyers cannot read the offer, and many more will not bother to squint. Put the type on a stable ground. Dark text on a light field, or light text on a dark field, with enough difference that the words survive sunlight on a phone.

Do not rely on color alone to carry a meaning. A red asterisk and a green check are invisible to a share of visitors, and they are easy to miss for everyone else. Pair the color with a word, an icon that has a label, or a pattern. Errors in a form should say what failed, next to the field, in text.

Size is part of contrast in practice. Body text that is cleverly small will fail people who enlarge the page, and it will fail people on a phone held at a normal distance. Let the browser's text resizing work. Layouts that clip or overlap when text is larger are broken layouts. The line length can stay comfortable while the type grows. A fixed-height hero that slices the headline is the usual failure.

Pictures of text are a trap. A slogan baked into an image cannot be resized cleanly, cannot be read by assistive tech unless you repeat it, and cannot be edited when the offer changes. Set the words in HTML. Let the image be the image.

## Focus and the keyboard path

Operable means a person can reach everything that matters without a pointer. Tab from the top of the homepage. You should see where you are at every stop. The focus style can match the brand. It cannot be removed because it looked busy in a screenshot.

The order should follow the reading order. Logo, primary navigation, the main action, then the rest. A skip link at the start lets a keyboard user jump past a long menu. On a short marketing page this feels like a small kindness. On a page with a large footer and a repeated header, it is the difference between using the site and giving up.

Menus, dialogs, and the cookie bar need an exit. Focus should move into a dialog when it opens and return to the button that opened it when it closes. It should not loop forever inside a menu, and it should not disappear onto a hidden element. Test this by keyboard alone, with the mouse unplugged or ignored. If you get stuck, the buyer will too.

The booking link, the form, and the playback control are the stops that matter most. A custom button built from a div, with a click handler and no key handler, will fail this test. Use a button or a link. Style it however the brand needs. The element is what makes it operable.

## Names, labels, and images

A control without a name is a silent button. Icon-only actions in the header, a close mark on a dialog, a play control on a showreel: each needs an accessible name a screen reader can speak. The visible tooltip is not always that name. Write the name in the markup.

Form fields need labels that stay visible. Placeholder text that vanishes on focus is not a label. "Work email" beside the field, or properly associated with it, tells the person what to type and tells the browser what to autofill. Group related fields when the form is more than three lines. Say what happens when they submit, in the button: "Book a call" rather than "Submit."

Images that carry meaning need alt text that describes the picture. A photograph of the product should say what is in the frame. Images that are purely decorative can be marked so assistive tech skips them. Do not stuff the alt text with the phrase you hope to rank for. The alt text is for a person who cannot see the file. Keyword packing is noise in their ear.

Video and audio need a transcript or captions when the words matter. A showreel that is only music and shots may not need a full caption track, but if the founder is speaking the offer, the offer has to exist as text too. Autoplay with sound is a separate failure. Let the visitor start the sound.

## A way to stop motion

Motion that runs on its own, or that answers every scroll with a new animation, makes some people sick and makes others lose the sentence. The page needs a way to stop that. The practical version on the web is to honor the system setting for reduced motion, and to avoid motion that was never explained in the first place.

Build the still page first. The headline is there. The sections are there. One animation may clarify a change of state, such as a menu opening. Everything else can appear without a dance. When the visitor has asked for reduced motion, serve the still version, not a slower version of the same chaos. Slower spinning is still spinning.

Do not make the sale wait for an intro animation. A logo that must finish before the headline appears has blocked the offer. If you keep a short sequence, cap it and give it a skip. People who clicked an ad, or followed a link from a friend, did not consent to a trailer.

Robust, the fourth principle, shows up here as markup that assistive tech can parse. Custom cursors, canvases that contain the whole page, and text drawn into WebGL scenes fail this quietly. They look sharp in a portfolio video. They are fragile on a real device with a real reader. Keep the offer in HTML. Use the fancy layer as an enhancement that can disappear.

## Put it in the brief

Name the bar before anyone opens a visual file. The page must be readable in sunlight, usable from a keyboard, labeled where a name is needed, and still when the visitor has asked for less motion. Those four lines belong next to the audience and the offer. They are not a footnote for the engineer to discover at the end.

Ask for the still version of every motion study. Ask which text sits on an image, and what the ground behind that text will be. Ask for the accessible names of the header icons in the same document as the icon drawings. A Figma frame can show focus, not only the hover state. If the focus ring is missing from the mock, it will be missing from the build until someone fights for it.

The robust principle is also a brief item. The offer stays in HTML. Illustrations and video can enhance it. They do not replace the sentence. When a vendor hands you a landing page as a single embedded canvas, treat that as a risk, not as a shortcut. You will struggle to meet a standard you can no longer edit as text.

## Review it without a lab

You can find the serious gaps in an hour. Tab through the homepage, a content page, and the form. Read every name your screen reader speaks for the header icons. Zoom the text. Turn on reduced motion and reload. Look at the page in grayscale and see whether anything essential vanished with the color.

Do this on a phone as well as a laptop. Focus and contrast failures hide in desktop screenshots, where the designer was close to a calibrated monitor. The buyer is outside, glancing. Hold the phone at arm's length. If the headline goes soft, it is not done.

Put the checks in the same list as the launch review. Contrast, focus, names, motion. They are not a follow-up ticket for a quieter month. A site can be fast and still be unusable. It can be beautiful and still hide the offer from the person who needed the plain version.

WCAG is a technical standard, and the W3C is explicit that the overview is not an introduction for its own sake. The success criteria are what conformance means. A small team can still start from the four principles and then check the criteria that match these failures. Aim at AA unless you have a reason to go further. Do not claim a badge you have not tested.

On a Hanabi project the page is built as HTML, styled with the same tokens as the brand, and reviewed on a keyboard before it is called done. That is ordinary craft. It is also what makes the site something a wider set of buyers can actually use.

See [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) if you want to judge how a public page carries type, image, and a clear next step together. The access checks are part of that standard, not a layer added for a proposal.

Long reading raises a narrower question inside the same principles: the measure of a line, the space between lines, and headings a person can scan. [Choosing type for a long article](/blog/choosing-type-for-a-long-article) is the next piece, because a page can pass a contrast check and still be tiring to read.
